questions.text: I can articulate the strategic direction of my organisation with precision — including the specific priorities, trade-offs, and time horizons that define it — without referencing documents or presentations.

I regularly identify patterns across market signals, competitive moves, and internal data that allow me to anticipate strategic challenges before they become visible to most others in my organisation.
I can hold the long-term strategic view and the near-term operational detail simultaneously — making decisions that serve both without sacrificing one for the other.
I find it difficult to explain how the work of my function connects to the broader organisational strategy in terms that are meaningful to people outside my domain.
I can clearly describe the two or three assumptions that, if proved false, would require our current strategy to change materially — and I monitor those assumptions actively.
When the organisational strategy changes significantly, I translate the implications into specific, actionable direction for my team without waiting for further guidance from above.
I have built organisational structures, role accountabilities, and performance rhythms that produce consistent results — even when I am not directly involved in day-to-day delivery.
I can describe a specific initiative I led in the past two years where I translated a complex strategic goal into a measurable operational outcome on schedule and within resource constraints.
My team often misses commitments or delivers below expectation even when the goal was clearly communicated — I find execution consistency difficult to sustain across my organisation.
I have a clear system for tracking progress against strategic priorities — one that gives me early warning when delivery is at risk, not just after the deadline has passed.
I hold accountabilities clearly across my organisation — people know precisely what they own, what success looks like, and what the consequence of non-delivery is.

I am comfortable making resource trade-off decisions — stopping or de-prioritising initiatives that are not delivering — rather than allowing underperforming programmes to continue consuming capacity.

I can articulate the specific mechanism by which my organisation creates value for customers and captures a portion of that value commercially — with enough precision to make credible resource allocation decisions.
I am comfortable interpreting financial statements and using financial data — revenue, margin, cash flow, unit economics — to make strategic and operational decisions in my domain.
I find commercial and financial conversations at the executive level difficult — I often rely on finance or commercial colleagues to interpret data before I can contribute meaningfully.

I understand the specific commercial dynamics of the APAC markets where I operate — including how pricing, customer relationships, channel structures, and competitive intensity differ from Western market norms.
I can make credible commercial decisions under uncertainty — recommending a course of action on pricing, market entry, or customer investment when the data is incomplete and the stakes are high.
I regularly use market intelligence — competitor moves, customer feedback, macro trends — to refine commercial direction, not just to confirm decisions already made.
I have deliberately built a team that is stronger than the sum of its individual members — where the team's collective capability exceeds what I could achieve by directing individuals separately.
I can identify at least two people in my current team who are on a trajectory to operate at my level or above within the next three years — and I am actively investing in that trajectory.
My team performs at a consistently high level when I am absent — they do not require my involvement in day-to-day decisions to maintain quality and pace.
I tend to be the primary decision-maker on most significant issues in my team — when I am not available, pace slows and quality varies noticeably.
I tailor my leadership approach to the individual — adjusting how I challenge, support, and develop each person based on their specific capability profile, motivation, and growth stage.
I have navigated difficult people decisions — performance management, restructuring, role elimination — in ways that preserved the trust and psychological safety of the broader team.
When market conditions shift significantly, I identify the strategic implications for my organisation before most peers or competitors do, and I act on those implications with appropriate speed.

I have successfully changed course on a significant strategic or operational initiative mid-execution — when new information made the original direction no longer viable — without losing stakeholder confidence in my leadership.
I perform at my best in stable, well-defined environments; when conditions are ambiguous or rapidly changing, my leadership effectiveness decreases noticeably.

I have led a team or organisation through a significant APAC regulatory, market, or stakeholder landscape shift — recalibrating strategy, structure, and priorities — while maintaining operational continuity.

I tend to maintain existing plans and commitments even when new information suggests the direction needs to change, because changing course in front of stakeholders feels like an admission of failure.
I can describe a specific instance in the past 12 months where I adapted my strategy or leadership approach in response to an external signal that others in my organisation had not yet acted on.
I have a clear framework for deciding which organisational decisions should be informed or supported by AI and which should remain under direct human judgment — and I apply it actively.

When AI-generated analysis conflicts with my own judgment or intuition, I have a disciplined process for evaluating which to follow — rather than defaulting automatically to either the AI output or my instinct.

I understand the data governance obligations that arise when AI is used in my organisation's decision-making processes — including who is accountable when AI-influenced decisions produce adverse outcomes.
I rely primarily on my technical colleagues to determine how AI should be governed in my organisation — I don't see AI governance as a core leadership accountability at my level.

I can articulate the specific ethical and reputational risks that AI deployment creates in my organisation's context — and I hold accountability for ensuring those risks are governed, not just identified.

I have led — or actively participated in — an organisational initiative to adopt or scale an AI tool or capability, including managing the change, resistance, and capability-building that adoption required.

archetypes.name: The Architect
archetypes.profile: High Strategic Thinking + High Adaptive Capacity, Advanced band
archetypes.core_strength: Designs robust systems and can pivot them when context changes. Rare combination at senior executive level.
archetypes.key_risk: Over-engineering; perfectionism slowing delivery; may underinvest in commercial urgency
archetypes.development_priority: Delegation discipline; "good enough" calibration; commercial acumen deepening

archetypes.name: The Catalyst
archetypes.profile: High Commercial Acumen + High Adaptive Capacity, Advanced band
archetypes.core_strength: Thrives in complexity and disruption; spots commercial opportunities others miss; acts fast
archetypes.key_risk: Impatience with process and governance; may burn out teams; can deprioritise people development
archetypes.development_priority: Sustainability mindset; team development investment; governance discipline

archetypes.name: The Diplomat
archetypes.profile: High People Leadership + High Strategic Thinking, Advanced band
archetypes.core_strength: Builds coalitions, navigates politics, aligns diverse stakeholders around complex strategy
archetypes.key_risk: May prioritise harmony over hard decisions; can be slow to confront underperformance
archetypes.development_priority: Decisiveness under pressure; constructive confrontation capability; execution rigour

archetypes.name: The Commander
archetypes.profile: High Execution Excellence + High Commercial Acumen, Advanced band
archetypes.core_strength: Delivers results through commercial discipline and operational rigour; highly credible in P&L conversations
archetypes.key_risk: May neglect people development for short-term results; can be directive at the expense of team capability-building
archetypes.development_priority: People leadership investment; long-term talent pipeline thinking; adaptive capacity

archetypes.name: The Navigator
archetypes.profile: High Adaptive Capacity + High People Leadership, Developing band
archetypes.core_strength: Guides teams through change with empathy and consistency; preserves team cohesion in uncertainty
archetypes.key_risk: May lack strategic direction or commercial edge; change leadership without destination clarity
archetypes.development_priority: Strategic thinking sharpness; commercial acumen; decision conviction

archetypes.name: The Strategist
archetypes.core_strength: Sees the big picture clearly; excellent at analysis and direction-setting
archetypes.key_risk: Execution gaps — vision without delivery mechanism; may rely on others for follow-through
archetypes.development_priority: Execution Excellence; team mobilisation; accountability architecture

archetypes.name: The Engine
archetypes.core_strength: Reliable delivery machine; consistent output; operationally credible
archetypes.key_risk: May be executing the wrong strategy; tends to optimise the current path rather than question it
archetypes.development_priority: Strategic thinking; commercial awareness; adaptive capacity

archetypes.name: The Entrepreneur
archetypes.profile: High Commercial Acumen + High Adaptive Capacity, Developing band
archetypes.core_strength: Bold commercial moves; market-savvy; pivots fast when opportunity shifts
archetypes.key_risk: May lack organisational buy-in or people development capability; governance gaps
archetypes.development_priority: People leadership; execution discipline; stakeholder management

archetypes.name: The Specialist
archetypes.profile: One dimension dominant (>15 pts above all others), any band
archetypes.core_strength: Deep expertise in one executive capability domain; highly valued for that specific strength
archetypes.key_risk: Over-reliance on single strength; may have blind spots in 2–3 other dimensions that limit seniority ceiling
archetypes.development_priority: Broadening capability across secondary dimensions; delegation of dominant strength to create capacity

archetypes.name: The Seedling
archetypes.core_strength: High development potential; early in the executive capability journey; typically high motivation
archetypes.key_risk: Overwhelm; pursuing development in too many areas simultaneously; wrong sequencing of priorities
archetypes.development_priority: Focus on 1–2 highest-leverage dimensions only; structured mentoring; SHIFT-QUEST programme indicated

bands.interpretation: Strong capability across all five dimensions; operating at senior executive level
1–2 capability gaps to address; strong foundation with targeted development needed
Substantive development needed in 2–3 dimensions; structured programme recommended
In transition to executive level; not yet operating at full capability
Fundamental capability gaps; foundational development required

bands.meaning: Deployable capability; executive operates at this level consistently and under pressure
Functional in stable conditions; gaps emerge under pressure or in unfamiliar APAC contexts
Underdeveloped for the executive's current or target role; primary development priority
